entities.summary:
The Black Death, also known as the Plague, was a pandemic that swept through Europe and other parts of the world in the 14th century, from 1346 to 1353. It is considered one of the deadliest pandemics in human history, causing the deaths of an estimated 75 to 200 million people, roughly 30-60% of Europe's population. The pandemic was caused by the bubonic plague, a highly infectious and deadly disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. The plague spread rapidly throughout Europe, fueled by trade routes, urbanization, and the lack of medical understanding and treatment. The pandemic had a profound impact on European society, leading to significant social, economic, and cultural changes.

The Black Death had a devastating impact on the social and economic fabric of Europe. It led to widespread poverty, famine, and social unrest, as well as a significant decline in the feudal system and the rise of a new class of landowners. The plague also had a profound impact on the arts and literature, with many writers and artists exploring the themes of mortality, suffering, and the human condition. Additionally, the plague played a significant role in the development of the Renaissance, as it led to a renewed focus on humanism and the study of classical texts.

The legacy of the Black Death can still be seen in modern society. The pandemic led to significant advances in medicine and public health, as well as the development of new technologies and social systems. It also had a profound impact on the way people thought about death and the afterlife, leading to a greater focus on individualism and the pursuit of happiness. As the famous historian and philosopher, Giovanni Boccaccio, wrote, "The plague has shown us that we are all equal in death, and that our wealth and status are of no consequence in the face of mortality."

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Black Death had a profound impact on the population of Europe, leading to a significant decline in numbers, and played a significant role in the development of the Renaissance and the modern era.

entities.summary: The bubonic plague pandemic (1347–1351) that killed 30–60% of Europe's population. The Black Death transformed European society by causing labor shortages, weakening feudalism, and accelerating the end of the medieval social order.
